units.la: DISPUTATIONUM THEOLOGICARUM SECUNDA, DE UNIVERSALITATE ECCLESIÆ:
units.tr: DISPUTATION 2 OF THEOLOGICAL DISPUTATIONS, ON THE UNIVERSALITY OF THE CHURCH:

units.la: In qua prima pontificiorum ecclesiæ nota falsitatis convincitur; &, neque illam, quæ se sub CATHOLICÆ nomine venditat, illico catholicam ac veram Christi ecclesiam; neque hanc, quæ á certis hominibus, tanquam novorum dogmatum architectis, invidiose denominatur ac traducitur, statim hæreticam esse, perspicuè ostenditur:
units.tr: In which the first mark of falsehood that the Papists attribute to the Church is refuted; and it is clearly shown that neither the body that puts itself forward under the name CATHOLIC is at once the catholic and true Church of Christ, nor is the body that is maliciously named and disparaged by certain men, as architects of new dogmas, at once heretical.

units.la: Postquam clarissima verbi divini face ac lucerna, ad quam f. Patres lucubravere, & sana ratio sine erratione discurrit, unicam, verissimam, evidentissimam, maximeq; propriam ac necessariam ecclesiae notam esse VERBI DEI COMMUNICATIONEM, aliis aetatibus aliis, divinis tamen, accidentibus vestitam, tanquam solem ex sole, demonstravimus, quae omnibus ad veram ecclesiam se aggregaturis non modo probabilitatis, sed & evidentiae ac necessitatis certitudinem ubertim faeneratur: jam quoq; ad eandem lucernam ostendemus, notas, quas pontificii ecclesiae affingunt, aut a nostris reveranon differre, aut non esse, aut non videri fi sunt, aut notas non esse si videntur, aut in sola voluntate esse imponentium, aut denique summe communia & incerta esse accidentia.
units.tr: Having shown, by the most clear torch and lamp of the divine Word, by which the holy Fathers laboured, and by sound reason that reasons without error, that the one, most true, most evident, most proper and most necessary mark of the Church is THE COMMUNICATION OF THE WORD OF GOD, clothed in different ways in different ages yet always in divine accidents, like sun from sun, which yields abundantly not only the certainty of probability but also of evidence and necessity to all who are about to join themselves to the true Church, we shall now show from the same lamp that the marks which the Papists attach to the Church either do not differ from ours, or are not what they claim, or do not appear to be what they claim, or are not marks at all if they seem to be, or exist only in the will of those who impose them, or are finally accidents that are very common and uncertain.

units.la: 2. Fastidita hic est, quam caeteroquin creberrime & ad ravim nobis objectant, sententiarum inter eos discrepantia de notarum numero qua materiali, qua formali, ut cum scholis loquamur, sive quae & quot illae sint. Praeterimus Jesuitas Posnanienses, qui numerant rant septem, Claritatem, 2. diffusionem seu amplitudinem, 3, antiquitatem, 4. apostolicæ ecclesiæ appellationem, 5. pastorum ordinem, & vocationem legitimam, 6, sanctitatem, 7. unitatem. Tacemus Horantium, qui contra Calvini institutionem Christianam scriptitans lib. 6. c. 6. unam duntaxat constituit notam, continuatam scilicet sacerdotum & prælatorum, præcipuè Romanorum, successionem. Non referimus Sotum, qui unitatem & concordiam vult præcipuam esse notam: non Lindanum, qui in panoplia sua dicit Romanum pontificem & cathedram Romanam esse indubitatam ecclesiæ notam: non cathechesin Synod. Trid., quæ duas tradit notas, quarum una est, quòd catholica sit, altera, quòd apostolica: non Hosium Cardinalem, qui quatuor notas proponit, 1. quod sancta sit, 2. quod catholica, 3. quod una, 4. quod apostolica: non Canisium, qui in catechismo suo hanc notam instar omnium facit, subesse scilicet Romano pontifici: non Sixtum senensem qui Vincentii Lirinensis tres notas repetit, nimirum ecclesiasticæ traditionis universitatem, antiquitatem & consensionem: non Sanderum, qui sex notas recenser, 1, altitudinem & sublimitatem, 2. splendorem & claritatem, 3. latitudinem & immensitatem, 4. successionem & perpetuitatem. fatem, . consensionem & unitatem, invi-ctam fidem & constantiam.
units.tr: 2. Here we pass over the disagreement of opinions about the number of marks, which they very often and tiresomely throw at us, whether material or formal, as we say in the schools, and what and how many these marks are. We pass over the Jesuits of Posen, who count seven: (1) clarity; (2) diffusion or extent; (3) antiquity; (4) the name of apostolic Church; (5) the order of ministers and their lawful calling; (6) holiness; (7) unity. We are silent about Horanti, who, writing against Calvin's Christian Institutes, book 6, chapter 6, sets up only one mark, namely the continued succession of priests and prelates, chiefly the Roman ones. We do not mention Soto, who wants unity and concord to be the chief mark; nor Lindanus, who in his Panoplia says that the Roman pontiff and the Roman chair are the undoubted mark of the Church; nor the Catechism of the Council of Trent, which gives two marks, one that it is catholic, the other that it is apostolic; nor Cardinal Hosius, who proposes four marks: (1) that it is holy, (2) that it is catholic, (3) that it is one, (4) that it is apostolic; nor Canisius, who in his catechism makes this one mark stand for all, namely subjection to the Roman pontiff; nor Sixtus of Siena, who repeats the three marks of Vincent of Lérins, namely the universality, antiquity and consent of ecclesiastical tradition; nor Sander, who lists six marks: (1) height and sublimity; (2) splendour and clarity; (3) breadth and immensity; (4) succession and perpetuity; (5) consent and unity; (6) unconquered faith and constancy.

units.la: Non Alexand. Pesantium Romanum, qui in 1. 2. d. Thom. q. 1. art. 1. disp. 5. Ecclesiam catholicam Romanam esse veram ecclesiam, atq; adeo ipsius Christi probat. 1. ex unitate 2. ex sanctitate, nimirum a parte principaliori, ratione multorum sanctorum qui in ea sunt: ratione sanctitatis, quam profitetur legibus & sacramentis: & qua est schola sanctitatis, & veritatis; docet enim & agit quae sancta sunt: quia habet caput sanctum saltem principale (papam enim quem pro ministeriali habet, non sanctum esse posse ficinnuit) quod est Christus: quia regitur a spiritu sancto ne erret in rebus fidei & moribus: propter sanctissima & varia divinae gratiae charismata, quib. ornata est, & ob universalia & efficacissima media sanctitatis, quibus divino beneficio abundat: quia Christi sanguine mundata & acquisita est: quia tota divino cultui dicata. 3. ex universitate, ratione cujus dicitur catholica. 4. ex eo qp sit apostolica.
units.tr: Nor do we mention Alexander Pesantius the Roman, who in 1 2 d. Thom. q. 1 art. 1 disp. 5 proves that the Catholic Roman Church is the true Church, and so of Christ himself: (1) from unity; (2) from holiness, namely from the chief part, on account of the many saints who are in it; on account of the holiness which it professes in its laws and sacraments, and by which it is a school of holiness and truth, for it teaches and does what is holy; because it has a holy head, at least a principal one (for he admits that the pope, whom it holds to be ministerial, cannot be holy), which is Christ; because it is ruled by the Holy Spirit lest it err in matters of faith and morals; on account of the most holy and various charismata of divine grace with which it is adorned, and on account of the universal and most effective means of holiness with which it abounds by divine benefit; because it has been cleansed and acquired by the blood of Christ; because it is wholly dedicated to divine worship. (3) from universality, by reason of which it is called catholic; (4) from the fact that it is apostolic.

units.la: Non Thomam Bozium, qui centum signa enumerat & explicat defumta ex triplici conjunctione ecclesiae cum Christo in unitate Spiritus per chrisma, in unitate corporis per eucharistiæ sacramentum, in unitate regni per sacramentum ordinis. Quin potius loquimur
units.tr: Nor do we mention Thomas Bozius, who enumerates and explains a hundred signs drawn from the threefold conjunction of the Church with Christ: in the unity of the Spirit through the chrism, in the unity of the body through the sacrament of the Eucharist, and in the unity of the kingdom through the sacrament of orders. Rather, we speak

units.la: quimur de Bellarmino, qui, ut fe numero puſgnare ostenderet, non veritate atq; virtute, quindecim notas totidem capitibus propo-nit,] . catholicæ ecclesiæ & Christianorum nomen, antiquitatem, durationem diuturnam, nec unquam interruptam, amplitudinem, five multitudinem & varietatem credentium, . successionem episcoporum in Romana ecclesia ab apostolis deducta usq; ad nos, ex qua dicitur apostolica, . conspiratio nem in doctrina cum ecclesia antiqua, unionem membrorum inter fe, & cum capite, , sanctitatem doctrinæ, , efficaciam doctrinæ, . sanctitatem vitæ auctorum fi-ve primorum patrum religionis Christianæ, , gloriam miraculorum, . lumen pro-phericum, .Confessionem adversariorum, . infelicem exitum, seu finem eorum qui ecclesiam oppugnarunt, . felicitatem illam temporalem, quæ divinitus collata est iis qui ecclesiam defenderunt. De Coffero, qui in enchiridio cap. 2, notas cudit duum generum, unum ab origine, alterum ab externis proprietatibus, sensu, ut loquitur, notiori-bus ex symbolo Coftantinopolitano aut potius apostolico petitum, cujuscemodi sunt unitas, , universitas, . sanctitas. De Socolo-vio, qui lib. 2. de discrimine veræ & falsæ ecclef, c. 1. notas distinguens in τεχμηρια necessario ecclesiam commonstrantia, quaecumque sacrum symbolum continet: & in σημείοις, quae etsi singula rem non demonstrant, multa tamen simul & veluti in unum cuneum collecta & conferta vincunt, qualia jam ex his jam ex aliis scripturae locis, sanctisque patribus & re adeo ipsa colliguntur, summatim enumerat viginti quatuor, quarum 1. est unitas, 2. sanctitas, 3. quod catholica, 4. quod apostolica, 5. praesentia spiritus sancti, 6. ad formas & species ejus in scriptura adumbratas convenientia & consensus, 7. filiae regis obedientia ad legem primam, hoc est, ad legem naturalem 8. ubertas donorum spiritus sancti, 9. incorrupta per omne aevum fundamentorum religionis Christianae conservatio, atque ejus documentorum, 10. veri cultus divini perpetua conservatio, 11. ordo a Christo Domino & ejus apostolis designatus & inchoatus, usque ad hanc aetatem integer conservatus, 12. communionis sanctorum sensus & consensus, 13. virtus miraculorum, 14. lumen & veritas prophetiae 15. praesens ubiq; & perenne Dei adjutorium, 16. opportuna ac salutaris correctio & depressio, 17. perpetuus in melius profectus, 18. novitatem omnem fugere, & suspectam habere, venerandae vetustati adhaerere, 19. extrema non sequi, medio tutissimam incedere, 20. perpetuum
units.tr: We speak of Bellarmine, who, to show that he fights by numbers rather than by truth and virtue, sets out fifteen marks under as many headings: the name of the catholic Church and of Christians; antiquity; long and unbroken duration; breadth, that is, the multitude and variety of believers; the succession of bishops in the Roman Church, traced from the apostles down to us, whence it is called apostolic; agreement in doctrine with the ancient Church; the union of the members with one another and with the head; holiness of doctrine; efficacy of doctrine; holiness of life in the authors or first fathers of the Christian religion; the glory of miracles; prophetic light; the confession of adversaries; the unhappy end of those who attacked the Church; and that temporal felicity which God has bestowed on those who defended the Church. Of Coffer, who in chapter 2 of his Enchiridion coins marks of two kinds, one from origin and the other from external properties, which he calls more evident to the senses, taken from the Constantinopolitan or rather the Apostles' Creed, such as unity, universality, and holiness. Of Socolovius, who in book 2 of his work on the difference between the true and false Church, chapter 1, distinguishes marks into proofs that necessarily show the Church [τεκμήρια], which are whatever the holy creed contains, and signs [σημεῖα] which, though no one of them demonstrates the thing by itself, yet together, gathered and packed like a wedge, prevail. He sums up twenty-four such signs, drawn now from this and now from that passage of Scripture, from the holy Fathers and from the thing itself: (1) unity; (2) holiness; (3) that it is catholic; (4) that it is apostolic; (5) the presence of the Holy Spirit; (6) agreement and consensus with the forms and patterns foreshadowed in Scripture; (7) the obedience of the king's daughter to the first law, that is, the natural law; (8) the abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; (9) the unchanged preservation through all ages of the foundations of the Christian religion and of its teaching; (10) the perpetual preservation of true divine worship; (11) an order designated and begun by Christ the Lord and his apostles, kept intact down to this age; (12) the sense and consensus of the communion of saints; (13) the power of miracles; (14) the light and truth of prophecy; (15) God's help, present everywhere and perpetual; (16) timely and salutary correction and restraint; (17) perpetual progress for the better; (18) to flee every novelty and regard it with suspicion, and to cling to venerable antiquity; (19) not to follow extremes but to walk in the middle, the safest course; (20) the perpetual [struggle]

units.la: Ἐ {t}uum contra illám omnium hæreticorum & schismaticorum bellum ac impugnationes. quod fit canon, regula omnis veritatis, & quod ultimò omnes hæretici ad eam provocent ac redeant, quod Deus ordinarit ex ejus ore audire gentes evangelium & credere, omnium ecclesiarum præsentis & præteriti temporis verissimum testimonium, apostasia, hæc autem est ab ea defectionis præsentiffima, tam publicè, quàm privatim Dei vindicta. -De Mulhufino deniq; , qui Bellarminum expilans disputat solam Romanam fidem esse veram doctrinam Christi, quia ex naturæ suæ conditione non habetà novis hominibus, diversorum nominum sectas. est antiquissima, una eademq; ab initio hucusq; la- tiffimè diffusa et catholica, ab antiquitate. ad nos successive deducta, confotmis pro- inde, primitivæ ecclesiæ, in qua ipsius pro- pugnatores universi unanimes sunt, quæ ethnicos convertit, quæ sanctos homines semper effecit, cujus alumni miracula ve- rafecerunt, quæ in verbum Dei non in- ficit manus, quæ arbitrarias & vertigino- fas scripturæ interpretationes aversatur, quæ omnibus hæresibus ostium claudit, quæ à blasphemis dogmatibus abstinet, cujus doctores, primi, medii, ultimi, in suis dogma-
units.tr: ...against that [faith] of all heretics and schismatics, which becomes the canon and rule of all truth, and to which all heretics at last appeal and return; that God has ordained that the nations should hear the gospel from its mouth and believe; the most true testimony of all churches of present and past time; apostasy, which is the most evident defection from it, and, both publicly and privately, God's vengeance. Finally, of Mulhufinus? No: of Mulhufinus, who, plundering Bellarmine, argues that the Roman faith alone is the true doctrine of Christ, because by the condition of its nature it does not draw its origin from new men or sects of various names; it is most ancient, one and the same from the beginning until now, most widely spread and catholic, handed down successively from antiquity to us, and accordingly conformed to the primitive Church, in which all its defenders are unanimous; which converts the heathen, which has always made holy men, whose pupils have worked true miracles; which does not lay hands on the Word of God, which shrinks from arbitrary and dizzying interpretations of Scripture, which closes the door to all heresies, which abstains from blasphemous dogmas, and whose teachers, first, middle and last, in their dogma-

units.la: dogmatibus persuadendis, nullis mendaciis indigent, & ab illis abstinent. Quas quidem ut ipse vult & vocat notas ego quoque in disputatione quadam Marpurgensi ante reti-nui, non quod eas pro γνησίοις ἢ ἰδιαίοις proprias ac vernaculis haberem, sed ut eas non pontificiorum proprias, sed & aliis communes, adeoque haud quaquam veras esse notas Mülhusino mihi suam ecclesiam veram esse persuadere frivole conanti demonstrarem.
units.tr: in persuading their dogmas, have no need of lies, and abstain from them. These marks, indeed, as he himself wishes and calls them, I too once maintained in a certain disputation at Marburg. I did not think them genuine or proper [γνησίοις ἢ ἰδιαίοις] and peculiar to the Church, but I wanted to show that they are not peculiar to the Papists and are common to others too, and so are by no means true marks, when Mülhusius was frivolously trying to persuade me that his church was the true one.

units.la: 3. Verum enim vero, ut deinceps ordinatim de singulis differam, nunc primam Bellarmini notam sumus examinaturi, ubi prius consideratum fuerit; An is ecclesiam catholicam recte coparavit cum sole, qui radios lucis clarissimos ex omni parte diffundat, ut facillime per eos dignosci possit?
units.tr: 3. But indeed, so that I may take up each point in order, let us now examine Bellarmine's first mark, after first considering this: Did he rightly compare the Catholic Church with the sun, which pours forth its most bright rays on every side, so that it can most easily be recognised by them?

units.la: 4. Hæc comparatio capite tertio a Bellarmino instituitur, at propriorum interibi oblito principiorum, ex quibus eam sicpote refellimus. Quæ res neq; in se, neq; in suis principiis videtur, ea non est similis soli radios lucis clarissimos omni ex parte diffundenti, ut facillime per eos cognosci possit. Atqui ecclesia vera neq; in se neq; in principiis suis (ex mente Bellarmini) videtur. Ergo ecclesia non est similis soli &c. Minor ita firmatur verbis Bell. Dicimus ergo notas ecclesia, quas C s afferes afferemus, non facere evidentiam credibilitatis.
units.tr: 4. Bellarmine draws this comparison in his third chapter, but he forgets its own proper principles, and so we refute it on those grounds. A thing which, neither in itself nor in its principles, appears to be like the sun pouring forth its brightest rays on every side, so that it can most easily be known by them, is not such a thing. But the true church does not appear like this, neither in itself nor in its principles (according to Bellarmine's mind). Therefore the church is not like the sun, etc. The minor premise is confirmed by Bellarmine's own words: We say, therefore, that the marks of the church which we bring forward do not produce evidence of credibility.

units.la: f. Quantum ad primam notam, status controversiae est: An quacunq; ecclesia nominatur catholica & christiana necessariò sit catholica & christiana: cui verò à certis dogmatum auctoribus nomina imponuntur, illico sit haretica?
units.tr: 5. As to the first mark, the state of the controversy is this: Is whatever church is called catholic and Christian necessarily catholic and Christian? And is the church which is given names by certain authors of doctrines at once heretical?

units.la: 6. Conclusio prima. Sicuti ecclesia eo quod catholicorum & Christianorum augustum nomen sibi arrogat, non illico est catholica & Christiana: ita nec illa, quae haereticorum titulis deturpatur, vel hominum alioqui in ea clarorum ac piorum nominibus traducitur, ea propter est haeretica. Haec vera est. quia nomina non semper ex certo judicio, sed ex communi more, & ex vulgi opinione, adeoq; saepe falso imponuntur. Praelustribus id claret exemplis. Templum in monte Garizim vocabatur verum Dei templum, Joh. 4. 20. Ecclesia Sardiensis dicebatur viva, quum mortua esset Apoc. 3. v. 1. Summi pontifices Judaeorum post Christum nomen retinebant sine re, uti hodie papistae dicuntur catholici, ut elucet ex Act. 23. v. 3. Simon Magus vocabatur μεγάλη δύναμις, non fuit tamen Act. 8. v. 10. Quaeigitur, quaesso, consequentiae ratio? Catholici vocamur. Ergo catholici sumus. quia ecclesiae catholicae nomen
units.tr: 6. First conclusion. Just as a church does not at once become catholic and Christian because it claims for itself the august name of Catholics and Christians, so neither is that church heretical which is disfigured with the titles of heretics, or which is otherwise branded with the names of men who were famous and pious within it. This is true, because names are imposed not always by sound judgement but by common custom and popular opinion, and so often falsely. The most famous examples make this plain. The temple on Mount Gerizim was called the true temple of God (John 4:20). The church at Sardis was said to be alive when it was dead (Rev. 3:1). The high priests of the Jews after Christ kept the name without the reality, just as the Papists today are called Catholics (as is clear from Acts 23:3). Simon Magus was called "the great power", yet he was not so (Acts 8:10). What, then, I ask, is the logic of this inference? We are called Catholics; therefore we are Catholics, because the name of the Catholic Church

units.la: 1 Ut ex Hieron. in Epist. 2 Ergo. [?]men non simul incepit cum ecclesia, adeo ab ea est separabile. Pacianus ep.1. ad Symp. ait, sub apostolis neminem vocatum fuisse catholicum. quia nomen sine actu atq; officio suo nihil est, teste Salviano lib. 4. de prov. Catholicus igitur non est qui vulgo vocatur, sed qui veritatem Dei, qui ecclesiam, qui Christi corpus diligit, qui divina religioni, qui catholicae fidei nihil praeponit, non hominis cujus quam auctoritatem, non amorem, non ingenium, non eloquentiam, non philosophiam, ut recte Vincentius Lirinensis in lib. contra prof. nov. c. 25. (scripsit. quia alioquin Ariani ac Donatistae forent catholici, qui se olim haud aliter catholicos, ac hodie papistae vocabant, ut patet ex Augustino & aliis. Unde concludimus cum Augustino tract. 5. in ep. Joh. Quomodo gloriaris te esse Christianum? Nomen habes & factum non habes. Si autem nomen sequutum fuerit opus; dicat te quisquam Paganum, tu factis offende te Christianum. Nam si factis non offendas te Christianum, omnes te Christianum vocent; quid tibi profuit nomen, ubi res non invenitur? Et cum Salviano, lib. 4. de providentia: Christianum nomen quasi aureum decus est, quo si indigne utamur, fiet ut sues cum ornamento esse videamur. Et cum ipso Bellarmino de notis eccles. c. 4. Omnis haeresis vult videri, & dici catholica.
units.tr: Just as from Jerome in his Epistle... The name did not begin at the same time as the church, and is so separable from it. Pacian, in his first letter to Sympronian, says that under the apostles no one was called catholic. A name without its act and office is nothing, as Salvian testifies in book 4 of On Providence. So the catholic is not the one who is commonly so called, but the one who loves the truth of God, the church, the body of Christ, who prefers nothing to divine religion or the catholic faith, and not the authority, affection, talent, eloquence or philosophy of any man. Vincent of Lérins rightly wrote this in his book against profane novelties, chapter 25. Otherwise the Arians and Donatists would be catholics, who called themselves catholics no differently from the way the Papists call themselves so today, as is clear from Augustine and others. Hence we conclude with Augustine, on the fifth tractate on the Epistle of John: How do you boast that you are a Christian? You have the name, but not the deed. If indeed the deed follows the name, let someone call you a pagan, and you will be offended by your deeds as a Christian. For if your deeds do not offend you as a Christian, everyone will call you a Christian; what has the name profited you where the reality is not found? And with Salvian, book 4 of On Providence: The Christian name is like a golden glory, which if we use it unworthily, it comes about that we seem to be swine with an ornament. And with Bellarmine himself, in On the Marks of the Church, chapter 4: Every heresy wishes to seem and be called catholic.

units.la: 3 quia nomen sine actu atq; officio suo nihil est.
units.tr: 3. Because a name without its act and office is nothing.

units.la: 4 quia alioquin Ariani ac Donatistae forent catholici. catholica ecclesia. Ubi tamen videtur in unâ eademque periodo ἀνλφαλκα protulisse scribens: Etiamsi omnis hæresis velit videri & dici catholica ecclesia, tamen quum interrogantur hæretici à Paganis, ubi ad catholicam convenient, nemo audet domum suam ostendere. Quasi vero hoc non ausos Donatistas queratur Augustinus, imò ipse fateatur Bellarminus de notis c. 1. Omnis, inquiens, hæresis ad se solam trahit veram ecclesiam, & alios omnes extra ecclesiam ponit. Nisi forte hic ecclesiam vult aliam esse veram, aliam catholicam. Ita & Ribera in Apocal. ostendit argumentationem à nomine ad rem esse infirmam. De ecclesia, inquit, Sardiensis dicit spiritus: scio opera tua, quia nomen habes quod vivis & mortua es. Apo. 3. Hæc erat mortua, quum tamen nomen haberet quod viveret, & opinione sua viva erat.
units.tr: 4. Because otherwise the Arians and Donatists would be catholics. Catholic church. Yet here he seems, in one and the same period, to have written an absurd slip: Even if every heresy wishes to seem and be called the catholic church, yet when heretics are questioned by pagans, where they gather to the catholic church, no one dares to show his house. As if Augustine were not complaining that the Donatists did not dare to do this! Indeed Bellarmine himself confesses it, in On the Marks chapter 1: Every heresy, he says, draws the true church to itself alone, and places all others outside the church. Unless perhaps here he means one thing to be the true church and another the catholic church. So also Ribera, in his commentary on the Apocalypse, shows that the argument from name to reality is weak: Concerning the church of Sardis the Spirit says: I know your works, that you have the name that you live, and you are dead (Rev. 3). This church was dead, though it had the name that it was living, and in its own opinion it was alive.

units.la: 7. Conclusio secunda.
units.tr: 7. Second conclusion.

units.la: Prima nota est ipsum catholica ecclesia & Christianorum nomen: nulla vero est hæresis quæ non accipiat nomen ab aliquo homine auctore suo, & nomen Christianum ius relinquat, à quibus discedit. Hæc est falsa, & Bellarmini. Coftero est secunda: Mulhusino, qui eam clepsit, item prima. Et quoniam hæc nota non est ἐγγεα-φῶν, ideo Bellarminus ad patres conversus in humana auctoritate sententiæ suæ præsidium quæriquæritat. . Augustinus lib. contra ep. fund. c. 4. sic scripsit: Quum omnes hæretici se catholicos dici velint, quærenti tamen peregrino alicui, ubi ad catholicam conveniatur, nullus hæreticorum vel basilicam suam, vel domum audeat ostendere. . Cyrillus Hierosolym. c. 18. catechef. scripsit: Si iveris in aliquam urbem, non petas ubi sit ecclesia, vel domus Dei: Nam etiam hæretici dicunt se habere domum Dei, & ecclesiam: sed petas ubi sit catholica ecclesia; id enim nomen proprium est hujus sanctæ ecclesiæ, matris omnium nostrum, Quasi dicat, si hoc quæras, nullus hæreticus suam ecclesiam ostendet. . Pacianus in epist. ad Symproni: quæ est de nomine catholico. Certe, inquit, non est ab homine mutuatum, quæ per secula tanta non cecidit. Catholicum ipsud nec Marcionem, nec Apellem, nec Montanum sonat, nec hæreticos sumit auctores. Et infra. Christianus mihi nomen est, catholicum vero cognomen; illud me nuncupat, ipsud ostendit. . Nullam esse hærefin quæ non accipiat nomen ab aliquo homine auctore suo & nomen Christianum iis relinquere, a quibus discedit, manifestum est, ex 1. Cor. 3. v. 4. ubi schismaticorum alii dicebant: Ego sum Pauli: alii, ego Apollo, alii, ego vero Cephæ. . Justinus in Tryphone: Et sunt, inquit, distincti cognominibus, denominati à quibusdam viris ut quisq;
units.tr: The first note is that the very name of the catholic church and of Christians: there is no heresy that does not take its name from some man as its author, and leaves the Christian name to those from whom it departs. This is false, and it is Bellarmine's claim. It is the second argument of Costerus, and Mulhusinus, who borrowed it, lists it first. Since this note is not written in Scripture [ἐγγεγραμμένη], Bellarmine turns to the Fathers and seeks support for his opinion in human authority. Augustine, in the book against the letter of Manichaeus (ch. 4), wrote: Although all heretics want to be called catholic, when some stranger asks where he may meet with the catholic church, no heretic dares to point out either his basilica or his house. Cyril of Jerusalem, in the eighteenth of his Catechetical Lectures, wrote: If you go into some city, do not ask where the church or the house of God is, for heretics too say that they have the house of God and the church. Ask rather where the catholic church is; for that is the proper name of this holy church, the mother of us all. As if to say: if you ask this, no heretic will point out his church. Pacian, in his letter to Sympronianus, on the name catholic: Surely, he says, it is not borrowed from a man, since it has not fallen for so many ages. The word catholic suggests neither Marcion, nor Apelles, nor Montanus, and it does not take heretics as its authors. And below: Christian is my name, catholic is my surname; the one names me, the other shows what I am. That no heresy takes its name from some man as its author, and leaves the Christian name to those from whom it departs, is plain from 1 Cor. 3:4, where some of the schismatics said: I am of Paul; others, I am of Apollos; others, I am of Cephas. Justin, in the Dialogue with Trypho: And they are distinguished, he says, by surnames, each named after certain men.

units.la: Quisquis fuit auctor alicujus nova doctrina, Ex iis alii vocantur Marcionitæ, alii Valentiniani, alii Basilidiani, alii Saturniniani, alii alio vocabulo, quisq; a primo inventore sui dogmatis. 6Irenæus lib. 1. cap. 20. Habent, inquit, & vocabula a principe impiissima sententia Simonis dicti Simoniani. 7 Lactantius lib. 4. c. 30. Quum Marcionita aut Arriani nominantur, Christiani esse desierunt, qui Christi nomine omisso, humana & externa vocabula induerunt. 8 Athanasius ferm. 2, contra Arrianos: Nunquam, inquit, populus abe piscopis suis, sed a domino in quem creditum fuit, nomen accepit; certe a beatis apostolis praeceptoribus nostris appellationes adepti non sumus, sed a Christo Christiani sumus, & nuncupamur: illi vero, qui aliunde fidei sua originem deducunt, merito auctorum suorum cognomena praeferunt. Quapropter quum a Christo omnes Christiani esse certamus, & dicere mur, explosus est Marcion inventor haeresis: reliqui autem qui remanserunt Christiani titulum retinuerunt: qui vero Marcionem sequuti sunt, iam non recte Christiani, sed Marcionitæ appellati sunt. Ita quoque Valentinus, Basilides, Manichaeus, & caeteri sectatoribus suis nomina impertierunt. 9 Chrysostomus hom. 33. in acta apostolorum: Illi habent quosdam a quibus appellantur, prout enim haeresiarcha nomen
units.tr: Whoever was the author of some new doctrine, from him some are called Marcionites, others Valentinians, others Basilideans, others Saturninians, others by some other name, each taking his name from the first inventor of his dogma. Irenaeus, book 1, ch. 20: They have names too, taken from the chief of the most impious opinion, Simon, called Simonians. Lactantius, book 4, ch. 30: When men are named Marcionites or Arians, they have ceased to be Christians, having dropped the name of Christ and put on human and external names. Athanasius, second sermon against the Arians: Never has a people received its name from its bishops, but from the Lord in whom it believed. We have not received names from the blessed apostles, our teachers; we are Christians and are named so from Christ. Those, however, who derive the origin of their faith from elsewhere rightly bear surnames taken from their authors. Therefore, since we all are Christians from Christ, and are so called, Marcion, the inventor of the heresy, has been cast out; but the rest who remained kept the title Christian. Those who followed Marcion are no longer rightly called Christians but Marcionites. So too Valentinus, Basilides, Manichaeus, and the others gave their names to their followers. Chrysostom, homily 33 on the Acts of the Apostles: They have certain men from whom they are named, for as the heresiarch is, so his name is

units.la: mens Men, ita etiam fella vocatur, nobis autem nullum vir nomen dedit, sed fides ipsa. 10. Hieronymus contra Luciferianos, in fine: Sic ubi audietis eos, qui dicuntur Christiani, non a Domino Iesu Christo, sed a quoquo alio nuncupari, ut Marcionitas, Valentinianos, scito non ecclesiam Christi, sed Antichristi esse synagogam. Iam vero, inquit, Bellar. Si nunc dicuntur alii Martinistae, vel Lutherani, alii Zwingliani, alii Calvinistae, &c. nos autem ab aliquo certo homine nemo unquam vocavit; constat nostram solum esse veram ecclesiam.
units.tr: Men [Manes], so too the sect is called; but to us no man has given a name, but the faith itself. Jerome, against the Luciferians, at the end: So when you hear those who are called Christians named not from the Lord Jesus Christ but from some other person, such as Marcionites or Valentinians, know that this is not the church of Christ but the synagogue of Antichrist. Now indeed, says Bellarmine: if some are now called Martinists or Lutherans, others Zwinglians, others Calvinists, and so on, but no one has ever called us by the name of some particular man, it is clear that ours alone is the true church.

units.la: 3. Solutio & vindicatio auctoritatum.
units.tr: 3. Solution and vindication of the authorities.

units.la: Ad primam. Augustinus nomen catholicae ecclesiae cum re conjunctum, non sejunctum nobis commendat, & ostendit ex solo nomine non recte colligi ecclesiae veritatem. Aitn. Omnes haeretici se catholicos dici volunt.
units.tr: To the first. Augustine commends the name of the catholic church as joined with the reality, not separated from it for us, and shows that the truth of the church is not rightly inferred from the name alone. You say: All heretics want to be called catholic.

units.la: Ad secundam. Cyrillus nostra notam approbat. Vocat enim ecclesiam καθολικὴν, διὰ τὸ διδασκειν καθολικῶς καὶ ἀνεπιτρως ἁπαντᾶν εἰς γνῶσιν ἀνθρώπων ἐλθεῖν ὀφείλοντας δογμάτων, i. e. quia docet catholice & perfecte omnia dogmata, quaecunq; homines tenentur cognoscere.
units.tr: To the second. Cyril approves our note. For he calls the church catholic [καθολικὴν], because it teaches catholically and completely all the doctrines that men are bound to know [διὰ τὸ διδασκειν καθολικῶς καὶ ἀνεπιτρως ἁπαντᾶν εἰς γνῶσιν ἀνθρώπων ἐλθεῖν ὀφείλοντας δογμάτων], that is, because it teaches all the doctrines that men are bound to hold, catholically and perfectly.

units.la: Ad tertiam. Pacianus item in solo nomine nullam certitudinem posuit, sed se nomine esse Christianum, cognomine catholicum, i. e. distingui cognomine hoc ab aliis qui se quoq; falso Christianos vocabant, stenIftendere conatus est. Quid? quod eo ipso nostram notam corroborat. Nam ad Sympron. Catholicus ait, ubiq; unum, velut doctores putant, obedientia omnium nuncupatur mandatorum scilicet Dei. Ergo qui catholicus idem obediens: qui obediens idem Christi-anus atq; ita catholicus Christianus est. Ad quartam. Omnem hærefin ab hæresis auctore nomen mutuari & falsum esse evincit historia, & auctoritate Paulina probari nequit. Non enim Corinthii propterea hæreticos fe obstringebant, quod præpofteroaffectu nunc hunc, nunc illum, nunc istum ex orthodoxis doctoribus ob donorum excellentiam præaliis sequendum ducebant. Ad quintam. Libenter concedimus, quod discit Juftinus Martyr, hæreticos esse distinctos cognominibus, quæ à suis auctoribus acceperunt. At nec omnes, necfoli. Nihiligitur hinc concluditur: Ad sextam, septimam, octavam, nonam & decimam. Nihil verius dici potuit à sanctis patribus in pravos illos hæreticos: verum rectius illud omne in papistas, quam reformatam quadrat ecclesiam. Non enim fastidito Christi nomine ab episcopis & doctoribus nostris gloriosa nomina habere gestimus, uti pars adversaria, nunc Benedictina, nunc Franciscana, nunc Jesuitica, nunc Cappucina audit propalam, & non fine gloriatione. Neq; Chryfoftomi, neq; Juftini, neq; hęq; ullius patris verba nobis sudes sunt in ꝏ tulis, uti suspicatus est Mulhusinus, sed ea ex veritate & recte sententiam scopo interpre- tamur & ampleƈtimur.
units.tr: To the third. Pacian likewise placed no certainty in the name alone. He tried to show that he was a Christian by name and catholic by surname, that is, that this surname distinguished him from others who also falsely called themselves Christians. What is more, he thereby strengthens our note. For in the letter to Sympronianus he says: the catholic is everywhere named the one who obeys all commandments, namely those of God. Therefore whoever is catholic is also obedient; whoever is obedient is also a Christian, and so the catholic is a Christian. To the fourth. History proves that it is false that every heresy borrows its name from its author, and Paul's authority cannot prove it. For the Corinthians did not bind themselves to heretics for this reason, that with a perverse fondness they now followed this man, now that one, now another of the orthodox teachers, thinking him to be preferred above the others because of the excellence of his gifts. To the fifth. We gladly grant what Justin Martyr says, that heretics are distinguished by the surnames they received from their authors. But not all, nor only these. Nothing therefore follows from this. To the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth. Nothing truer could have been said by the holy Fathers against those wicked heretics; but all of it fits the Papists far better than our reformed church. For we do not scorn the name of Christ and boast of glorious names taken from our bishops and teachers, as the adversary party does, which is openly and not without boasting called now Benedictine, now Franciscan, now Jesuit, now Capuchin. Nor do we take the words of Chrysostom, Justin, or any other Father as our rules in matters of faith, as Mulhusinus suspects; but we interpret and expand their opinions from the truth and in accordance with the scope of Scripture.

units.la: 9. Conclusio tertia. Illa est vera ecclesia, qua catholica est, h.e. per totum orbem terrarum ac per omnia tempora fusa. Ratio ⁊. quia hanc notam maxime ex omnibus universa sacra commendat & celebrat scriptura. Talis enim revera ecclesia quaerenda est, qualis primis patriarchis promissa est, qualem prophetae adumbrarunt: qualem Christus ipse ejus fundator futuram esse praedixit. Atqui primo Abrahae talis ecclesiae status promittitur, Gen. 22. v. 17. 18. Haaco Gen. 26. v. 3. 4. Jacobo Gen. 28, v. 3. 4. Talem futuram praedixerunt prophetae Psal. 72, v. 8. 9. 10. Psal. 2. v. 8. & 22. v. 28. & 19. v. 9. & 80. v. 9. Esaias non tam adumbrat, quam vivis coloribus tam amplos ejus fines depingit c. 60. v. 3. 6. & f. 54. v. 1. Adde quod de lapide universam terram occupante est Dan. 2. Mich. 2. Zach. 9. Mal. 1. idem Christus docuit Marc. 16. Act. 1. Luc. 24. Matth. 24. Act. 2. quia hac universa antiquitas limites verae ecclesiae amplissime contra omnes haereticos semper tutata est, ut intelligitur ex Irenaeo, ex Tertulliano, ex Augustino, ex Hieronymo, ex Paciano, ex aliis.
units.tr: 9. Third conclusion. That is the true church which is catholic, that is, spread throughout the whole world and through all times. Reason. Because Scripture as a whole commends and celebrates this mark above all others. For the church must be sought in the form in which it was promised to the first patriarchs, in which the prophets foreshadowed it, and in which Christ himself, its founder, foretold that it would be. Now, to Abraham first, the state of such a church is promised: Gen. 22:17, 18. To Isaac: Gen. 26:3, 4. To Jacob: Gen. 28:3, 4. The prophets foretold such a church: Ps. 72:8, 9, 10; Ps. 2:8; Ps. 22:28; Ps. 19:4; Ps. 80:9. Isaiah does not so much foreshadow it as depict its wide borders in lively colours: Isa. 60:3, 6; Isa. 54:1. Add that the stone filling the whole earth is in Dan. 2; Mic. 2; Zech. 9; Mal. 1. Christ himself taught the same: Mark 16; Acts 1; Luke 24; Matt. 24; Acts 2. Because all this antiquity has most amply guarded the limits of the true church against all heretics, as is understood from Irenaeus, Tertullian, Augustine, Jerome, Pacian, and others.

units.la: 10. Solutio. Haec conclusio Socolovii D
units.tr: 10. Answer. This conclusion of Socolovius D—

units.la: vera quidem est, at extra quæstionis præfentis ambitum. Aliud enim est, fi quæras; An vera ecclesia fit catholica, id quod nemo unquam ex nostris negavit; aliud vero fi quæras, An nomen catholicæ ecclesiæ fit certa & vera nota ecclesiæ Christi, id quod hactenus negamus, & deinceps negaturi sumus. Tota igitur Socolovii disputatio hic est supervacanea. Præterea universalitas licet aliquomodo accidat veræ ecclesiæ: tamen ejus nota non est, tum quia non est sensilis, tum quia non inest ei semper, id quod veritas etiam Coftero Jesui-tæ invito extorsit in enchiridio suo pag. 89. ita scribenti: In apocalypsi prædixit apostolus novissimis temporibus cœlum recessurum ad interfectionem libri involuti, b. e. ecclesiam quæ prius late patebat in angustiis contrahendam. Quanquam is eam nihilominus catholicam tum fore ibidem affirmet.
units.tr: is indeed true, but it lies outside the scope of the present question. For it is one thing to ask whether the true Church is catholic, which no one among us has ever denied; it is another to ask whether the name of the catholic Church is a certain and true mark of the Church of Christ, which we have hitherto denied and shall go on denying. So Socolovius's whole disputation here is superfluous. Moreover, although universality does in some way belong to the true Church, it is not a mark of it, both because it is not perceptible to the senses and because it does not always belong to it. Truth itself wrested this from the Jesuit Costerus, against his will, in his Enchiridion, p. 89, where he writes: In the Apocalypse the apostle foretold that in the last times the heaven would be withdrawn for the destruction of the book that was rolled up, that is, the Church, which previously spread widely, would be drawn into narrow limits. Although he nevertheless affirms in the same place that it will then be catholic.

units.la: II. Conclusio quarta. Hæretici sunt qui a certis dogmatum auctoribus nomina trahunt.
units.tr: II. Fourth conclusion. Heretics are those who take their names from certain authors of doctrines.

units.la: Ita concludit J. Mulhufinus p. 2. disp. de fide thef. 2. Verum, inquiens, ne longius abeamus ipsa Lutheranorum, Zuinglianorum, Calvinistarum & similium qui perpetuo novi suppullulant, nomina satis magnam, de suspecta doctrina significationem dant. Semper enim ab ipsis ecclesiæ incunabulis, quia a certis quibusdam hominibus denominati fuissent, hæretici ab orthodoxis deprehensi sunt: ut Nicolaitæ, Apo. 2. Arriani, Eunomiani, Novatiani &c. Unde et Iustinus Martyr, ex iis, inquit, alii vocantur Marcionitæ, alii Valentiniani, Basilidiani, alii Saturniniani, alii alio vocabulo, quisque a primo inventore sui dogmatis (Iust. in dialogo cum Tryph.) Et Chrysostomus illi (haeretici) habent quosdam a quibus appellantur, prout enim haeresiarchæ nomen, ita & secta vocatur. Chrysost. hom. 33. in Act. Apost.
units.tr: So concludes J. Mulhusinus, p. 2, disp. de fide, thesis 2. "But," he says, "not to go further afield, the very names of the Lutherans, Zwinglians, Calvinists and the like, who keep sprouting up new, give a great and suspicious indication of their doctrine. For from the very cradle of the Church, whenever heretics were named after certain men, they were detected as such by the orthodox, as the Nicolaitans (Rev. 2), Arians, Eunomians, Novatians, etc. Hence also Justin Martyr says: "From these, some are called Marcionites, others Valentinians, Basilidians, others Saturnilians, others by another name, each taken from the first inventor of his doctrine" (Justin, in the Dialogue with Trypho). And Chrysostom: "Those heretics have certain men from whom they are named; for just as the name of the heresiarch is, so the sect is also called." Chrysostom, homily 33 on the Acts of the Apostles."

units.la: 12. Solutio. Mülhusinum ita nec reformatæ ecclesiæ doctores haereseos convincere, neque Romanæ fidei sectatores a schismatis aut erroris nota liberare sic ostendo. 1. Qui a certo dogmatum auctore nomen trahit, is est haereticus, ex hypothesi Mülhusinia. Atqui olim omnes fideles Antiochia a certo dogmatum auctore nomina trahebat. Nam Sycophanta Tertullus evangelicam professionem odiose nominabat hærefin Nazarenorum, a Jesu Nazareno, servatore nostro, Act. 24. v. 5. Ergo olim omnes fideles erant haeretici. Falsa & medax est conclusio. Ergo aliqua ex præmissis. Non minor. Est enim Spiritus sancti. Igitur major, quæ est Jesuitæ. Discere igitur Sophista distincte loqui de dogmatis veri propugnatore & haereseos auctore: Et audi Lindanum vestrum in præfat. Panoplias. Prisci, inquit, seculis catholicæ fidei propugnatores, Basilium, Nazianzenum, Ambrosium, Hieronymum, Augustinum, haereticī, haereticos, Manichæos, Homoiousianos
units.tr: 12. Answer. I show in this way that neither the teachers of the reformed Church can be convicted of heresy by Mulhusinus, nor can the followers of the Roman faith be freed from the mark of schism or error. 1. He who takes his name from a certain author of doctrines is a heretic, on Mulhusinus's hypothesis. But all the faithful at Antioch once took their names from a certain author of doctrines. For the sycophant Tertullus used to call the evangelical profession, spitefully, "the heresy of the Nazarenes," from Jesus of Nazareth, our Saviour (Acts 24:5). Therefore all the faithful were once heretics. The conclusion is false and lying; so one of the premises is false. The minor is not. Indeed it is the Spirit of the Holy One's. So the major, which is the Jesuit's, is. Let the sophist learn therefore to speak distinctly about a defender of true doctrine and the author of a heresy. And hear your Lindanus in the preface to his Panoplia: "The ancient defenders of the catholic faith in former ages, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, were called heretics, Manichaeans, Homoiousians

units.la: {1} Cf. the marginal annotations on the Antiochian sect.
units.tr: {1} See the marginal notes on the Antiochian sect.

units.la: Sanistas, Sabellianos, Basilianistas appellabant. Nos Calvini, Zwinglii & aliorum Christi servorum nominibus invidiose traducimur & calumniose, quum tamen nec in Calvinum, nec in Zwinglium, neq; in alium ullum credamus, neq; in eorum vel aliorum verba aut facta juremus, sed & ubi exerrarunt, ab eis discedere sumus paratissimi, pios interim eorum labores, quibus papanam δαιμονιῶν & idololatriam detexerunt & destruxerunt, ad Dei cultum usurpates. Audi Lutherum tom. 4. vol. germ. sol. 4. Sunt qui se Lutheranos esse gaudent: non sic, o fatue, non sic, oro, ut meum numen taceatur, & nemo Lutheranus, sed Christianus appelletur. Quid est Lutherus? doctrina non est mea, neq; pro vobis crucifixus fuit. D. Paulus, se 1. ad Cor. 3. nolebat pati ut Christiani dicerentur a Paulo, sed a Christo. Unde igitur mihi fatido vermium sacco accederet, ut filii Christi a meo vilissimo nomine denominarentur? Absit! Q amici! deleamus schismatica nomina, & denominetur Christus, cujus doctrinam habemus. Audi Bellarminum Calvini & Lutheri advocatum lib. 3. de verb. Dei c. 3. protestantes tenent spiritum non esse alligatum ullis episcopis aut ulli hominum generi: & Johannes Calvinus omnium hominum, atq; adeo cochlearum definitiones ad amussim scripturarum examinari jubet: & Lutherus, non ulli homini, nequit, committum est ut cotendat aut constituat, quid sit.
units.tr: Sabellians and Basilians." We are slandered and maliciously traduced by the names of Calvin, Zwingli and other servants of Christ, although we believe neither in Calvin, nor in Zwingli, nor in any other, and we swear to the words or deeds of neither them nor others; and where they went astray, we are most ready to depart from them, while we use their pious labours, by which they uncovered and destroyed the Papacy, the demons' and idolatry, for the worship of God. Hear Luther, vol. 4 of the German edition, fol. 4: "There are those who rejoice to be called Lutherans. Not so, you fool, not so, I beg you, that my name be kept silent and no one be called a Lutheran but a Christian. What is Luther? The doctrine is not mine, nor was I crucified for you. St Paul, 1 Cor. 3, would not allow himself to be called a Christian by Paul, but by Christ. Why then should the stinking sack of worms come to me, that the sons of Christ be named from my vile name? Far from it! O friends, let us erase the schismatic names, and let Christ be named, whose doctrine we have." Hear Bellarmine, the advocate of Calvin and Luther, On the Word of God, book 3, ch. 3: "The Protestants hold that the Spirit is not bound to any bishops or to any class of men; and John Calvin orders that the definitions of all men, and even of snails, be examined by the rule of the Scriptures; and Luther, that it is committed to no man to judge or determine what is."

units.la: II. Qui à certis dogmatû auctorib9 nomina trahût, sunt haeretici. Atqui Carmelitae, Benedictini, Dominicani, Franciscani, Cappacini, Jesuitae, Lojolae impia proles, à certis dogmatum auctorib9 nomina trahût. Singuli enim habent singulas vivendi regulas, singulas religiones, à caeteris discretas. Etau forte haec regulę pro dogmatis non sunt habendae? Igitur hi omnes sunt haeretici, ex sententia Mulhusini. Sed, inquit Mulhusinus, nullus Franciscanus ab Augustiniano aut Carmelita à Benedictino, aut Benedictinus à Dominicano &c. in fidei dogmatibus differt, ut Lutherani à Calvinianis, hi ab Anabaptistis, & à Flacianis, isti et singuli ab omnib9 et invicem. Egregiû certę veritatis divinae κεφαλαιον! Hominum scilicet variorum uniformis deliritas. Satis igitur nobis sit ad ὀρθοδοξίαν fidei nostrae afferendam, licet totus mund9 discreparet, f. scripturae exquisita harmonia. Haec norma, haec regula nobis certissima. Verum ut reliquarum monasticae impietatis sectarum nullam nunc attingam, videamus quomodo Jesuitae cum caeteris imo cum scripturis conspirent, vel in hoc uno capite, nim. de causa peccati. De hac vestrū dogma audite ex Bellarmino lib. de grat, & lib. arbit. c. 8. qui ita inquit: Respondeo, primum hominem no sua culpa fuisse casurum, quoniam Necessitas aliquando cadendi fuisset et naturalis. Audis hominem non casurum. fuisse sua culpa, sed ex necessitate, quia ejus natura ita condita fuerit, ut non posset non cadere. Si vero necessitate naturæ ita condit³ homo non potuit non cadere, & à vita excidere, utiq; conditor naturæ, auctor est lapsus & ruinæ istius: ideoq; non plus peccarunt nostri parentes peccando, quàm ignis peccat uredo: imò necaliter adhuc hodie homo peccabit, quàm ex necessitate, & expers omnis culpæ, nec aliter quàm culpa ex Deo, & ex solo Deo, ô blasphemiam! ô impietatem! Ita Durandus vester sine pudore, Deû asserit causam peccati, teste eodem Bellarmino lib. 2. de amis. grat. c. 18. Scilicet hoc didicistis ex patre vestro Simone, non Petro, sed mago, qui eandem vobiscum habuit fidem. Ita enim Bell. vester de eo testatur: Simon magus nō docebat aperte, Deum velle, seu imperare aut etiam efficere mala; sed ea ratione peccatorum nostrorum causam esse, quod eam naturam nobis dederit, quæ non possit nō peccare, lib. 2. de amis. grat. c. 12. Si Simon magus propter hanc doctrinam pro hæretico est habedus (utiquest suo meritissimo) quid nunc Romanensis ecclesia aliud est quam asylū & domicilium omnium istorum hæreticorum? Sic, sic excutite sinum vestrum, Jesuitæ, & aliis sanioribus scabiem hanc vestrā aclepram affricare definite! Porrò Mulhusinus obsecrat nos ut edicam⁹ quis reformatorum sit, qui magis sit à Christo, q ab homine aliquo novo, quiq; novam aliq; sectam intriverit, nomesortiatur? Christiani, inquit, cer-te a Christo dici nequeunt. Audiant enim Lactan-tium. Quum Marcionitæ & Arriani (Calvinistæ aut Lutherani) nominatur, Christiani esse desie-runt.lib.4.c.30. Sed quid hoc contra nos? Nos veritatem naturæ humanæ Christi, contra Marcionitas, ac divinæ veritate, contra Arrianos, fortiter defendimus. Frustra igitur in causa impari hisjudicamur pares. Hæc tamen injuria nobis erit mus-fitanda, quum orthodoxi Patres eandem olim forte fuerint experti, ut nuper probavimus ex Lindano. Et hic probe cogitetur, quod Arias Montanscripsit in c.26. Matth. Nazareni nomen tam infame apud Judæos esse caperat propter Jesum, quæ NOVÆ SECTÆ auctore distinctabant, eratque perinde ac sibi-reticum qs diceret. Etsi Papistæ vel maxime a nullo certo auctore nomina acceperunt, tamen ideo catholici non effent. Recte enim Alphonsus de castro: Surrexerunt, inquit, Acephali, qui simul insurgebant: nullus enim repertus est, qui eorum esset princeps et magister. Tales & sunt Alogiani, Ignoeitæ, Anthropomorphitæ, Angelici, Anabaptistæ, Cathari, quibus nulla persona, sed suæ hæreses nomina indiderunt. Sed nulla unquam secta rectius a ducibus suis, quam potificii ipsi a papa cognomen suum hauserunt. Nam Ederus Oecon. bibl.lib.5.in epilogo: Catholicus est (inquit Lyrinensis) qui veræ fidei no præponit cujus quam auctoritatem. At pontificiorum confessio est, Catholicus est, qui est uni pastori papæ subdit, Bell.lib.3.de eccles. mil.c.2. Cujus summi pastoris voci obsequendum est, teste Stapleton, &c.
units.tr: II. Those who take their names from certain authors of doctrines are heretics. But the Carmelites, Benedictines, Dominicans, Franciscans, Capuchins, Jesuits, the impious offspring of Loyola, take their names from certain authors of doctrines. For each has its own rules of life and its own religious observances, distinct from the others. Or perhaps these rules are not to be counted as doctrines? So all of these are heretics, on the view of Mulhusinus. But, says Mulhusinus, no Franciscan differs from an Augustinian or a Carmelite, nor a Benedictine from a Dominican, etc., in the doctrines of faith, as Lutherans differ from Calvinists, these from Anabaptists and Flacians, and each of these from all and from each other. A remarkable summary of divine truth indeed! Namely, the uniform folly of various men. It is enough for us, then, to vindicate the orthodoxy of our faith, even if the whole world disagreed, the exquisite harmony of Scripture. This is our most certain norm, our rule. But, to leave aside the rest of the monastic impious sects, let us see how the Jesuits agree with the others, indeed with the Scriptures, even in this one point, namely the cause of sin. Hear your dogma on this from Bellarmine, On Grace and Free Will, ch. 8, who says: "I answer that the first man was not going to fall through his own fault, since the necessity of falling was at some time natural." You hear that man was not going to fall through his own fault, but from necessity, because his nature was so constituted that he could not but fall. But if by the necessity of nature man was so constituted that he could not but fall and go out of life, then surely the Creator of nature is the author of that fall and ruin. Therefore our parents did not sin by sinning any more than fire sins by burning; indeed even today man will sin, not less from necessity, and free of all fault, and not otherwise than by fault from God, and from God alone. O blasphemy! O impiety! So your Durandus, without shame, asserts that God is the cause of sin, as the same Bellarmine testifies, On the Friendship of Grace, book 2, ch. 18. Surely you learned this from your father Simon, not Peter, but the magician, who had the same faith as you. For your Bellarmine bears witness of him thus: "Simon Magus did not openly teach that God wills, or commands, or even effects evil; but by this reasoning he taught that He is the cause of our sins, because He gave us a nature which cannot not sin," On the Friendship of Grace, book 2, ch. 12. If Simon Magus is to be held a heretic for this doctrine (and rightly so), what else is the Roman Church now but an asylum and home of all these heretics? Shake out your bosom thus, Jesuits, and cease to rub this leprous scab of yours onto the saner sort! Further, Mulhusinus urges us to say which of the reformers is more from Christ than from some new man, and which, having introduced a new sect, takes its name? "Christians," he says, "certainly cannot be called from Christ. For let them hear Lactantius." When Marcionites and Arians (Calvinists or Lutherans) are named, they have ceased to be Christians (book 4, ch. 30). But what has this to do with us? We strongly defend the truth of Christ's human nature against the Marcionites, and of his divine nature against the Arians. Therefore we are judged equals in an unequal cause in vain. Yet this injury must be borne by us, since the orthodox Fathers perhaps experienced the same in former times, as we have just shown from Lindanus. And let this also be carefully considered, what Arias Montanus wrote on Matthew 26: the name Nazarene had begun to be so infamous among the Jews because of Jesus, whom they distinguished by the author of a NEW SECT, and it was just like calling someone a heretic. Although the Papists, most of all, have received their names from no certain author, they would not on that account be catholic. For Alphonsus de Castro rightly says: "There arose the Acephali, who rose up together, for no leader or master of theirs was found. Such also are the Alogians, Ignorants, Anthropomorphites, Angelici, Anabaptists, Cathari, to whom no person gave a name, but their heresies did." But no sect ever took its name from its leaders more justly than the Papists took their name from the pope himself. For Eder, in his Oeconomia Bibliorum, book 5, in the epilogue: "A catholic is (says Vincent of Lérins) one who prefers the authority of no man to the true faith." But the confession of the Papists is: "A catholic is one who is subject to the one shepherd, the pope," Bellarmine, On the Church Militant, ch. 2. To this voice of the supreme shepherd, as Stapleton testifies, obedience must be given, etc.

units.la: §. Fons huj9 erroris eit, quòd adversarii nö attendút 1. discrimen inter DICI&ESSE. Multa n• dicuntur,quæ nõ sunt:&multa sunt,quæ non di• cütur.2.Discrimen inter nomé catholicum & ejus rationem. Nomen est nimis commune. Omnis n• hæresis vult videri & dici catholica, teste Bellar•mino. Ratio nominis est triplex. Dicitur n.catho• lica 1. de universalitate doctrina, quam profitetur de Deo, de creaturis, de angelis &c. Secundo, de uni• versalitate loci, quia per universum orbem terrarum diffusa est. Tertio respectu temporis quia ad finem mundi perseverabit, ut annotat Valentia Analyf. lib. 6. c. 3. Si primam examines, nostra doctrina non minus est Catholica, quam vestra. Hanc e• nim rationem Sozomenes lib. 7. c. 4. sic explica• vit. Theodosius, inquit, decrevit, ut illorum eccle• sia dumtaxat catholica diceretur, quæ trinitatem æquali honore coleret. Si secundam, Romana Ca• tholica nunquam fuit. Cofterus Jesuita in en• chir. cap. de eccles. ut, inquit, ecclesia eodem tem• pore totius orbis ditiones occupet. ne in hunc usq; di• em forte contigit, quando Antarctici hominibus, & qui extremas remotissimas America oras in• colunt, fides Christi nunquam innotuit, p. 89. Et sane si hæc ratio valeat, Judæorum & Epicuræo• rum cætus per orbem dispersus catholicæ ec• clesiæ tandem referet. Et deniq; si tertiam, non magis est catholica, quam ecclesiæ malignatium & ipse mundus.
units.tr: The source of this error is that our opponents do not attend to two points. First, the distinction between what is said (dici) and what is (esse): many things are said that are not so, and many things are so that are not said. Second, the distinction between the name catholic and the reason for it. The name is far too common: every heresy wants to be seen and called catholic, as Bellarmine testifies. The reason for the name is threefold. It is called catholic (1) from the universality of the doctrine it professes concerning God, creatures, angels and so on; (2) from the universality of place, because it is spread through the whole world; and (3) with respect to time, because it will last until the end of the world, as Valentia notes in his Analysis, book 6, chapter 3. If you examine the first sense, our doctrine is no less catholic than yours. Sozomen, book 7, chapter 4, explained this very reason in this way: Theodosius, he says, decreed that only the church that worshipped the Trinity with equal honour should be called catholic. If you take the second sense, the Roman Catholic church has never been catholic. Costerus the Jesuit, in his Enchiridion, chapter on the church, says that the church should occupy at one and the same time the dominions of the whole world; "and perhaps this has not happened even to this day, when the faith of Christ has never become known to the people of the Antarctic and to those who inhabit the most remote shores of America," p. 89. And indeed, if this argument holds, the assembly of Jews and Epicureans dispersed throughout the world will at last belong to the catholic church. And finally, if you take the third sense, the church of the wicked is no more catholic than the world itself.
